contributions.statement: If tools are retrieved per sub-task from a large catalog, the main failure is the planner splitting the task into the wrong number of steps (larger models over-split more). Feeding the retrieved candidate names back into one re-planning pass fixes step count, but top-1 tool choice stays near 40%, so expose the top ~10 candidates rather than a single pick.
contributions.evidence: §7.5-7.6, Table 2: SAD DA 51.0→67.7% (n=300, p<1e-6); 14B over-decomposes (4.72 vs 2.94 GT steps); oracle step count gives CatR@1 39.8% vs CatR@10 79.1%; on DA-matched queries SAD adds nothing (p=0.97).

contributions.statement: Listing ~100 tool names in the prompt gives worse top-1 tool-category choice than per-step retrieval, even for a much larger model.
contributions.evidence: §7.3, Table 2: qwen-max with 100 names CatR@1 21.1% vs 37.0% for 7B + SAD; 50 queries, single run, names only, mixed sample sizes.

reason: One qualifying nuance survives: the step-granularity bottleneck and the top-1 ceiling, backed by a significance-tested oracle control. It applies only to catalogs of hundreds to thousands of tools, so for a ≤15-tool Java host it transfers indirectly. The expose-all claim is weak and duplicates stronger KB tool-retrieval papers.
